newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian heavy fuel oil exports seen stable to high.
newsitem.headline: Russian heavy fuel oil exports seen stable to high.

text.p: Traders gave varying assessments on Monday of Russian heavy fuel oil exports this summer, with some saying peak season deliveries could double from certain outlets and others seeing stable volumes.
But most sources agreed the bulk of deliveries would go through the Baltics, with less material heading out through the Black Sea to a competitive refinery market.
"It's quite a bit more this year," said one Western trader, referring to volumes of heavy fuel oil, known as mazut, out of St Petersburg.

"We'll at least double the volume on last year," he said, adding St Petersburg, the major outlet to northwest Europe, had exported 700,000-800,000 tonnes in the eight or so weeks since the main export season opened in May.

But a second trader put the volume out of Petersburg over May and June at 1.05 million tonnes, including 700,000 tonnes last month alone. "There is no reason to expect this will not continue," he said.

A third estimate put Petersburg at 400,000 tonnes per month on storage vessels and an additional 200,000 tonnes per month through the port, with Russia's average total monthly mazut exports at about 1.53 million tonnes.
Traders had said earlier that Russia's total monthly mazut exports over the peak season could hit 1.8 million tonnes from all outlets.

"We're seeing a high volume of both straight run and cracked coming out -- the European and U.S. markets are absorbing a lot and it's supporting netbacks in Russia," the third trader said. "We'll see stable and maybe increased volumes."
He put monthly deliveries at 130,000 tonnes via Ventspils and 250,000 tonnes through Klaipeda, up 50-60 percent on 1996 levels.

The Black Sea port of Novorossiisk would do 300,000 tonnes per month while its cousin Odessa would export 200,000 tonnes monthly, he said. Deliveries by the Volga Tanker fleet and other barges would be 50,000 tonnes per month.

One trader said deliveries from Arkhangelsk and Kandalaksha were falling short of expectations, with the latter having done only 35,000 tonnes in June. Another put deliveries out of Ventspils at 300,000 tonnes per month.

"There's not that much coming out of the Black Sea -- it's one or two cargoes here and there," said the first trader. "People have understood it's better to take it to the Baltics -- it's easier to find a home for it, because there's a lot of competition for refineries in the Med."

Traders said strong prices, steady refinery output and growing sophistication among Russian oil companies were underpinning exports, which they saw split evenly between straight run and cracked material.

"Probably people have learned the financing schemes," said one Western trader, adding deliveries were less jumpy than in previous years. "The big majors like LUKoil are better organised, from logistics to marketing. They know a bit more this year."
There are fewer players in the Russian mazut export market, with two companies controlling the bulk of trade, sometimes on behalf of other traders, out of St Petersburg.

Domestic refineries have had an easier time with runs recently, since stable domestic crude oil prices have made it easier to plan feedstock purchases. Russian refineries make no profit on mazut exports below $70 or so a tonne cif NWE.

But Russia exports mazut at almost any price, given the vast quantities of the heavy product it produces. Still, one trader said that if prices dipped to $70-$75, Russia could drastically cut exports.
Russia's peak mazut export season runs from approximately May through October, after which outlets freeze and deliveries drop sharply.
